vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: using exactly the same words, with nothing changed
the main thing you should remember from a meeting
the written record of what was said and decided in a meeting

to understand something that was not said directly
to make something weaker or less strong than it was

paras: Priya Nandakumar has taken the minutes of other people’s meetings for thirty years, and she says the question she is asked most often is the one with the least useful answer. People want to know how she gets it down word for word. She does not, and she would refuse if anybody insisted. “Verbatim minutes are a bad document,” she says. “Nobody speaks in finished sentences. Write down exactly what an intelligent person said in a meeting and they come out sounding confused, and then the reader spends the afternoon judging the speaker instead of the decision.”

So she paraphrases, and she is careful about how. When somebody says they are on track, she writes that they said they were on track, attributed to them by name. When somebody promises to send figures on Friday, she writes that he said he would send them on Friday. When a question is asked, it goes in without the question mark: she asked whether the filing had been submitted. It is a small transformation, done forty or fifty times an hour, and she describes it as the least interesting skill she has and the one that has kept her employed.

There is one thing she never touches. If somebody agrees with a condition attached, the condition goes in as close to the original words as she can manage. “A caveat that gets tidied up stops being a caveat. That is the single most common way minutes go wrong, and almost nobody does it on purpose. You write he agreed, because that is the shortest true thing, and the sentence has just watered down the whole conversation.” She has seen decisions made months later on the strength of an he agreed that had four words missing from the end of it.

Her other rule costs ten seconds and prevents most of the arguments. Before anybody leaves the room, she reads the decisions back out loud. Not the discussion — the decisions, and any conditions on them. People correct her about one time in five, usually about something small, and the correction is free. “A correction in the room takes ten seconds,” she says. “A correction by email, after I have circulated it to forty people, takes three days and an argument, and somebody always ends up defending a position they did not know they had taken.”

What she will not do is pretend the document is neutral. Somebody chose which of the ninety things said in that hour were the four worth writing down, and that somebody was her. “The takeaway is a decision I make. I try to make it the same one the room would have made. But anybody who tells you the minutes are just a record has never written any.”
reading.source: A composite portrait of a professional minute-taker, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how to take minutes quickly enough to keep up with a meeting.
To show that reporting somebody accurately means choosing what to change and what to leave exactly as it was said.
To argue that meetings should be recorded rather than written up.

listenings.text: I have been taking minutes for a very long time and the question I get asked most is how I write it down word for word. I do not, and I would argue with anybody who asked me to. Verbatim minutes are a bad document. Nobody speaks in finished sentences. If you write down exactly what an intelligent person said in a meeting, they come out sounding confused, and then whoever reads it spends the afternoon judging the speaker instead of looking at the decision. So I paraphrase. There is one thing I never paraphrase, and it is a condition. If somebody agrees with a caveat, that caveat goes in as close to the original words as I can manage, because a caveat that gets tidied up has stopped being a caveat, and nobody ever does that on purpose. You write he agreed, because it is the shortest true thing you can write, and you have just removed the four words that mattered. And here is the habit that prevents most arguments. Before anybody leaves the room, I read the decisions back out loud. A correction in the room takes ten seconds. A correction by email, after I have sent it to forty people, takes three days and an argument.

There is an experiment from the nineteen thirties that has never really stopped being run. A psychologist gave people an unfamiliar folk story to read once, and then asked them to retell it from memory. Then he gave that retelling to the next person, who retold it to the next, down a chain. Nobody was trying to change anything. Everybody was doing their honest best to pass on what they had received. Two things happened, and they happened every single time. The story got much shorter. And the parts that did not match what the listeners expected either quietly disappeared or turned into something familiar. Details that made no sense to them were not preserved as strange details. They were replaced by ordinary ones. Now apply that to an organisation, because this is where it stops being a curiosity. A warning with a condition attached to it goes from the person who found the problem to their manager, to a summary, to a slide, to somebody very senior. And the thing that goes first, at every single step, is the condition. What arrives at the top is a clean recommendation with no caveat on it, and if you go back down the chain looking for the person who removed it, there is nobody there. Everybody simplified slightly, and the sum of slight simplifications is a different message.
